nameStory: The name 'devil's bit' comes from the plant's thick, stubby rootstock that looks like it was bitten off short. Folk legend claimed the devil bit off the end of the root in anger because the plant was too useful to humans as medicine. The scientific name Chamaelirium means 'ground lily,' referring to its low rosette of leaves.
description: Devil's bit is a unique perennial wildflower that grows from a basal rosette of smooth, oval leaves about the size of your palm. From this ground-hugging cluster emerges a single tall spike covered in tiny white or yellowish flowers, reaching up to 4 feet tall on female plants. It's a rare member of the lily family that you might mistake for a completely different plant when it's flowering versus when it's just leaves. The plants are either male or female, with the females growing much taller spikes but having fewer flowers.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Six or so smooth, oval leaves arranged in a flat rosette at ground level, each about 3-6 inches long with prominent parallel veins and a slightly waxy feel

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny white to pale yellow flowers densely packed on a narrow spike; female spikes much taller and more sparse, male spikes shorter and fluffier with more flowers

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Single flower spike emerges from center of ground-level leaf rosette, creating a distinctive 'fairy wand' appearance

idTips.label: Stem
idTips.description: Smooth, unbranched flowering stem that feels sturdy and slightly ridged when rolled between your fingers

habitat: Devil's bit grows in moist, rich soils of deciduous woodlands and wet meadows throughout eastern North America. In New England, look for it in partially shaded areas with consistent moisture, often in the same habitats where you'd find trilliums and wild ginger. It prefers slightly acidic soils and is most commonly found at lower elevations in areas that don't completely dry out in summer.

seasonality.spring: Basal rosette of leaves emerges early, looking like a small hosta or plantain at first glance. The distinctive leaf arrangement and waxy texture become apparent as leaves fully expand.
seasonality.summer: Flowering spike emerges in late spring to early summer, with the dramatic height difference between male and female plants becoming obvious. This is the best time for positive identification.
seasonality.fall: Leaves may persist into early fall before dying back, while seed capsules develop on female plants.
seasonality.winter: Plant dies back completely to underground rootstock, leaving no above-ground traces.

funFact: Female devil's bit plants are such demanding mothers that they often skip flowering for years at a time to recover their energy, which means in any population you'll find about ten male plants for every female - an extremely unusual gender ratio in the plant world!
confusionNotes: The leaf rosette can be confused with plantain or small hostas, but devil's bit leaves have a distinctive waxy feel and prominent parallel veining. When flowering, it's unmistakable - no other New England plant produces such a tall, narrow spike of tiny flowers from a ground-level rosette.
contextualKnowledge: Despite its common name 'blazing star,' this plant is completely unrelated to the purple blazing stars (Liatris species) that bloom in late summer. The shared name causes confusion among wildflower enthusiasts, so always check the scientific name when reading about blazing stars.
compareHints: Devil's bit is the only species in its genus, making it truly unique. Within its family, it's most similar to bunchflower (Melanthium) but differs dramatically in having a ground-level leaf rosette rather than stem leaves, and much smaller individual flowers. The rosette growth form combined with the tall flower spike makes it unmistakable among New England lilies.
